site.name: Boulder Canyon Hydroelectric Project / Barker–Kossler System
overview: The Boulder Canyon Hydroelectric Project linked Barker Reservoir, a roughly 12-mile gravity pipeline, Kossler Reservoir, a high-pressure penstock and a powerhouse in Boulder Canyon. Completed in 1910, it used the large elevation drop from the mountains to generate electricity while moving water through the system.

The project became an important early high-head hydroelectric development in Colorado. The same infrastructure later became central to Boulder's municipal water supply, and the city purchased the Barker system in 2001.

timeline.text: An early proposal sought to harness Middle Boulder Creek for a large hydroelectric plant, but the first effort did not proceed.
Property at Barker Meadows was acquired for the reservoir and a successor power company began construction of Barker Dam and the Boulder Canyon hydroelectric works.

More than a thousand workers built the gravity pipeline across steep Boulder Canyon terrain. The line used three-foot reinforced-concrete pipe, tunnels, retaining walls and temporary construction camps.
The hydroelectric plant entered operation. City history records an initial full-power output of about 10,000 kilowatts.
The project's generating capacity was expanded to roughly 20,000 kilowatts.
The City of Boulder purchased the Barker system from Public Service Company of Colorado, bringing the reservoir, pipeline and related hydroelectric facilities under city ownership.

moreHistory: Water traveled from Barker Reservoir through the Barker Gravity Pipeline to Kossler Reservoir, then descended through a steel penstock to the Boulder Canyon powerhouse. The steep drop created the pressure needed for high-head hydroelectric generation.

Construction required extensive blasting, temporary camps, aerial tramways and large-scale pipe production. City records describe dangerous work conditions and document injuries and fatalities during construction.

The Barker system remains active infrastructure. It now serves both municipal water-supply and hydroelectric functions, so Remnant presents the historic system as an industrial landscape rather than implying unrestricted access to individual operating facilities.
